subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 68-year-old woman who underwent radical mastectomy 8 years ago has developed long-standing, refractory lymphedema of the left arm. Over several months, ill-defined purple plaques and nodules appear on the edematous arm skin. Biopsy shows an infiltrative malignant vascular neoplasm. She has a history of radiation therapy to the chest wall.
question: Which of the following best describes this presentation?

options.text: Kaposi sarcoma associated with HHV-8 and HIV
Bacillary angiomatosis caused by Bartonella infection in AIDS
Cutaneous angiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves syndrome) arising in chronic postmastectomy lymphedema
Pyogenic granuloma triggered by local trauma
Cherry angioma, a benign capillary hemangioma of middle age

explanation_correct: Angiosarcoma is a rare, aggressive blood vessel malignancy that typically occurs on the head, neck, and breast of older adults on sun-exposed skin. It is associated with radiation therapy and with chronic postmastectomy lymphedema; angiosarcoma developing in chronic lymphedema is called Stewart-Treves syndrome. Hepatic angiosarcoma is linked to vinyl chloride and arsenic exposure. These tumors are difficult to resect because diagnosis is often delayed. This woman's postmastectomy lymphedema and radiation history make Stewart-Treves angiosarcoma the diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Kaposi sarcoma is an HHV-8-associated endothelial malignancy seen with HIV or transplantation, typically with lymphocytic infiltrate, not an aggressive tumor in a lymphedematous postmastectomy arm.
explanation_incorrect.B: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign Bartonella-induced capillary papule eruption in AIDS with a neutrophilic infiltrate, not an infiltrative malignancy in lymphedema.
explanation_incorrect.D: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign polypoid lobulated capillary hemangioma associated with trauma or pregnancy, not an aggressive tumor arising in chronic lymphedema.
explanation_incorrect.E: Cherry angioma is a benign capillary hemangioma that appears in middle age, increases with age, and never regresses; it is not a purple infiltrative plaque.

educationalObjective: Cutaneous angiosarcoma occurs on sun-exposed head/neck/breast in older adults and can arise in chronic postmastectomy lymphedema (Stewart-Treves syndrome).

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 42-year-old man with poorly controlled HIV (CD4 count 60 cells/uL) develops multiple violaceous plaques and nodules on his skin and oral mucosa, along with similar lesions discovered in the GI tract on endoscopy. Histology shows a spindle-cell endothelial proliferation with a prominent lymphocytic infiltrate.
question: Which infectious agent is most strongly associated with this condition?

options.text: Human herpesvirus 8 (KSHV)
Bartonella henselae
Low-risk human papillomavirus
Epstein-Barr virus
Varicella-zoster virus

explanation_correct: Kaposi sarcoma is an endothelial malignancy associated with HHV-8 (KSHV) and HIV. It classically affects older Eastern European males, patients with AIDS, and organ transplant recipients. It involves skin, mouth, GI tract, and respiratory tract, and histology shows a lymphocytic infiltrate, unlike bacillary angiomatosis, which has a neutrophilic infiltrate. This patient's HIV, mucocutaneous and GI involvement, and lymphocytic infiltrate are classic.

explanation_incorrect.B: Bartonella causes bacillary angiomatosis, a benign capillary papule eruption with a neutrophilic infiltrate that can mimic Kaposi sarcoma but is not a true malignancy.
explanation_incorrect.C: Low-risk HPV causes verrucae with koilocytosis and condyloma acuminatum, not an HHV-8-associated endothelial malignancy.
explanation_incorrect.D: Epstein-Barr virus is associated with hairy leukoplakia, Burkitt lymphoma, and infectious mononucleosis, not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanation_incorrect.E: Varicella-zoster virus causes varicella and zoster, a vesicular exanthem and dermatomal reactivation, not an endothelial tumor.

educationalObjective: Kaposi sarcoma is an HHV-8/HIV-associated endothelial malignancy of skin, mouth, GI and respiratory tracts with a lymphocytic infiltrate.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 35-year-old woman with AIDS and a CD4 count of 30 cells/uL develops numerous small, benign-appearing red capillary papules on her trunk and face. The eruption closely resembles Kaposi sarcoma clinically, but biopsy reveals a neutrophilic infiltrate rather than a lymphocytic one. She is treated with antibiotics and the lesions regress.
question: Which of the following is the most likely cause and distinguishing feature of this eruption?

options.text: HHV-8 with a lymphocytic infiltrate and visceral involvement
Epstein-Barr virus producing white plaques on the lateral tongue
Staphylococcus aureus producing honey-colored crusted lesions
Bartonella infection producing a neutrophilic infiltrate and frequently mistaken for Kaposi sarcoma
Pseudomonas aeruginosa producing ecythma gangrenosum-like lesions

explanation_correct: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign capillary skin papule eruption seen in patients with AIDS, caused by Bartonella infection. It is frequently mistaken for Kaposi sarcoma, but the key distinguishing feature is a neutrophilic infiltrate on histology, whereas Kaposi sarcoma has a lymphocytic infiltrate. The benign vascular papules and response to antibiotics fit this patient. The other options describe different organisms or different inflammatory patterns.

explanation_incorrect.A: HHV-8 with a lymphocytic infiltrate describes Kaposi sarcoma, a true endothelial malignancy, not a benign antibiotic-responsive eruption.
explanation_incorrect.B: Epstein-Barr virus causes hairy leukoplakia, white painless plaques on the lateral tongue that cannot be scraped off, not capillary papules.
explanation_incorrect.C: Staphylococcus aureus causes impetigo with honey-colored crusts or a walled-off abscess, not a neutrophilic vascular papule eruption in AIDS.
explanation_incorrect.E: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is not the cause of bacillary angiomatosis and would not produce this benign capillary papule picture with neutrophilic infiltrates.

educationalObjective: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign Bartonella-induced capillary papule eruption in AIDS with a neutrophilic infiltrate, mimicking Kaposi sarcoma.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 35-year-old woman has a small red-blue nodule beneath the nail of her right index finger. The lesion causes severe, paroxysmal throbbing pain that is triggered by cold exposure and pressure. It has been slowly enlarging but remains localized.
question: Which of the following best describes this lesion?

options.text: A benign capillary hemangioma of infancy that will spontaneously involute
A benign, painful red-blue tumor arising from modified smooth muscle cells of the thermoregulatory glomus body
A malignant vascular tumor associated with radiation and chronic lymphedema
A cauliflowerlike wart caused by low-risk HPV with koilocytosis
A benign capillary hemangioma of middle age that does not regress

explanation_correct: A glomus tumor is a benign, painful, red-blue tumor that commonly occurs under the fingernails. It arises from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a thermoregulatory structure, which explains the cold sensitivity and severe pain. The subungual location and paroxysmal pain are characteristic. It is benign and distinct from the painless capillary hemangiomas listed in the other choices.

explanation_incorrect.A: Infantile hemangioma appears in the first weeks of life and involutes after age 1; it is not a painful subungual nodule in an adult.
explanation_incorrect.C: A malignant vascular tumor associated with radiation and lymphedema is angiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves syndrome), not a small painful glomus tumor.
explanation_incorrect.D: A cauliflowerlike wart with koilocytosis is a verruca from low-risk HPV, not a painful red-blue glomus tumor.
explanation_incorrect.E: A benign capillary hemangioma of middle age that does not regress is a cherry angioma, not a painful subungual lesion.

educationalObjective: Glomus tumor is a benign painful red-blue subungual tumor derived from modified smooth muscle of the thermoregulatory glomus body.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 28-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy develops a rapidly growing, bright red, polypoid and lobulated nodule on her gingiva. It ulcerates and bleeds profusely after minor trauma while brushing her teeth. She reports no pain and has no known malignancy.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Cherry angioma
Infantile hemangioma
Kaposi sarcoma
Glomus tumor
Pyogenic granuloma

explanation_correct: Pyogenic granuloma is a polypoid, lobulated capillary hemangioma that can ulcerate and bleed, and it is associated with trauma and pregnancy. This patient's rapidly growing lobulated gingival nodule that bleeds after minor trauma during pregnancy is classic. The lesion is benign despite its alarming appearance and name. Hormonal and traumatic triggers explain the association with pregnancy and local injury.

explanation_incorrect.A: Cherry angioma is a benign, flat to slightly raised capillary hemangioma appearing in middle age that does not regress and does not typically ulcerate or bleed.
explanation_incorrect.B: Infantile hemangioma appears in the first weeks of life, grows rapidly, and involutes after age 1; it is not a lesion of pregnancy.
explanation_incorrect.C: Kaposi sarcoma is an HHV-8-associated endothelial malignancy with lymphocytic infiltrate, not a benign lobulated bleeding nodule of pregnancy.
explanation_incorrect.D: Glomus tumor is a small painful red-blue nodule derived from the glomus body, usually under a fingernail, not a painless bleeding gingival nodule.

educationalObjective: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign polypoid lobulated capillary hemangioma linked to trauma and pregnancy that ulcerates and bleeds easily.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: Parents notice a bright red vascular lesion on their 3-week-old infant's cheek. It grows rapidly over the first few months, then begins to shrink and fade when the child reaches 1 year of age. The parents ask how this compares with the small red spots that appear on adults as they age.
question: Which of the following statements best distinguishes these two types of hemangioma?

options.text: Both infantile hemangiomas and cherry angiomas spontaneously involute by age 1
Cherry angiomas appear in the first weeks of life and involute, whereas infantile hemangiomas do not
Infantile hemangioma appears in the first weeks of life, grows rapidly, then involutes starting at age 1, whereas cherry angiomas do not regress
Both are painful red-blue tumors arising from the glomus body under the fingernails
Infantile hemangioma is an HHV-8-associated endothelial malignancy of infancy

explanation_correct: Infantile hemangioma is a benign capillary hemangioma of infancy that appears in the first few weeks of life, initially grows rapidly, and then involutes starting at age 1. Cherry angioma is a benign capillary hemangioma that appears in middle age, increases in frequency with age, and never regresses. The key contrast is that infantile hemangiomas spontaneously involute while cherry angiomas cannot. This infant's lesion appearing at 3 weeks and involuting at 1 year fits infantile hemangioma.

explanation_incorrect.A: Only infantile hemangiomas involute; cherry angiomas do not regress, so the two are not the same in this respect.
explanation_incorrect.B: The timing is reversed: infantile hemangioma appears in early infancy and involutes, while cherry angioma appears in middle age and persists.
explanation_incorrect.D: Painful red-blue subungual tumors from the glomus body are glomus tumors, not either type of capillary hemangioma.
explanation_incorrect.E: Infantile hemangioma is benign and not associated with HHV-8; HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma.

educationalObjective: Infantile hemangioma appears in early infancy, grows, then involutes after age 1; cherry angioma appears in middle age and never regresses.
